Lesson 2 · Understand the problem

Distributions and association

The repaired file gives us a trustworthy overall rate. The director now needs to know which parts of the chain create the largest service problem.

Business question → General theory → Worked application → Synthesis

First learn the definitions, notation, and logic of the method. Then use the shared case to work through the calculation and its interpretation.

Read here or present the same material, one step at a time.

The motivating question

The chain cannot give every store the same amount of operational attention. The next decision is where to investigate first. We will turn the weekly records into one baseline average per store, examine the spread of those averages, and compare delivery-time groups. The result is a review shortlist and a clearer description of the workload that an alert program would face.

Connect the foundations before calculating

General theory

A countable set of opportunities gives probability its denominator

Fictional teaching table: one randomly selected product-day from these 100
Delivery groupAvailableStockoutTotal
Short54660
Long281240
Total8218100

Each product-day belongs to exactly one row and one outcome column. Define A as a stockout and L as long delivery. A probability here is a count divided by the number of eligible opportunities. P(A)=18/100=.18. This describes this finite table; using it to forecast another setting requires a stability argument. The table is an illustration, not an additional estimate from the shared chain.

Conditioning changes the denominator to the named group

The bar means “among”; “and” retains the whole-table denominator
QuestionCalculationAnswer
P(stockout)18/10018%
P(stockout | long)12/4030%
P(stockout | short)6/6010%
P(stockout and long)12/10012%

Read P(A|L) aloud as the probability of A among L. Restrict the table first, then calculate the share. The joint probability P(A and L)=.12 combines membership and outcome. The conditional probability .30 uses only the 40 long-delivery opportunities. Neither the notation nor a difference between groups implies that changing delivery would cause the difference.

An expected value is an average with probability weights

Y={1stockout0otherwiseE[Y]=0×0.82+1×0.18=0.18

Y names a numerical outcome before a product-day is selected. E means its probability-weighted average across possible values. The formula Σ yP(Y=y) means multiply each possible value by its probability and add; Σ is an instruction to sum. An expectation need not be an outcome any single unit takes. For a zero-or-one indicator it equals the event probability. For a cost or duration it retains the units of that variable.

Conditional means recombine using population shares

E[Y∣short]=0.10;E[Y∣long]=0.30E[Y]=0.60×0.10+0.40×0.30=0.18

E[Y|X=x] is the average outcome in the group named by x. Recombine the two means by the shares of opportunities in those groups. A simple average of .10 and .30 would implicitly give each group half the weight. If the long-delivery share changes to .75 while the conditional risks stay fixed, the overall mean becomes .25. This is the same weighting logic later used in standardization.

A conditional association does not identify an intervention effect

  • Independence would make the conditional probabilities equal
  • Here 30% differs from the overall 18%
  • Other group differences can explain the association
  • In Lesson 3, the estimate itself varies across samples

For these binary events, independence requires P(A|L)=P(A) when P(L)>0; equivalently the joint probability equals P(A)P(L). This table fails that condition. For numerical variables, zero correlation alone does not imply independence: a symmetric U-shaped relationship is a counterexample. Keep extensive distribution families and Bayes calculations in the optional appendix. The required foundation is counts, conditional comparisons and weighted averages.

Describe a distribution before comparing groups

General theory

Exploratory analysis asks about centre, spread, shape, and relationships

  • Inspect units, missingness, and unusual values
  • Describe the typical value and variation
  • Look for clusters, asymmetry, and tails
  • Compare groups and relationships using consistent definitions

Exploratory data analysis builds an understanding of the observed distribution before selecting a model. Start with the observation unit and variable scale. A table supplies exact values; a graph exposes patterns. Together they help determine which summary answers the question and which features need further explanation.

Empirical and theoretical distributions describe different objects

  • Empirical distribution: frequencies in the observed data
  • Random variable: a numerical outcome of an uncertain event
  • Probability distribution: possible values and their probabilities
  • Expected value: a probability-weighted average

An empirical distribution assigns weight to the values actually observed. A theoretical distribution is a model for possible outcomes under repetition. Discrete probabilities add across values; continuous probabilities correspond to areas under a density. This distinction connects descriptive statistics with the later theory of sampling.

The mean and variance summarize location and squared spread

x¯=∑ixin;s2=∑i(xi−x¯)2n−1

The mean uses every observation and is sensitive to extreme values. Sample variance measures squared deviations from that mean, using n−1 when estimating a population variance from a sample. Its square root, the standard deviation, returns to the original measurement units.

Quantiles describe the distribution through ordered positions

  • Median: the 50th percentile
  • Q₁ and Q₃: the 25th and 75th percentiles
  • IQR = Q₃ − Q₁: spread of the middle half
  • Range: the observed minimum to maximum

Quantiles answer questions about positions in an ordered distribution. They complement mean and standard deviation when extreme values have strong influence. The median describes the middle observation, while the interquartile range describes how far the middle half extends. Always distinguish observed spread from uncertainty about an estimated mean.

Read and design a statistical display

General theory

Purpose, encoding, scales, and annotation make a graph readable

  • Purpose: name the comparison the reader should make
  • Encoding: use position, length, or area consistently
  • Scaffolding: label axes, units, scope, and denominators
  • Annotation: identify the pattern that answers the question

Choose the question before the chart. A histogram describes one numerical distribution; grouped boxes compare distributions; a scatterplot compares paired numerical values; a 100% stacked bar compares category shares. Use a table for precise values and a graph for patterns. Common scales support comparisons across panels. Labels and annotations should explain the relevant feature without obscuring the observations.

Frequency, relative frequency, and density use different vertical scales

Count=nj;share=njndensity=njn×bin width

Absolute frequency counts observations in a bin. Relative frequency divides by the total count. Histogram density additionally divides by bin width, so bar area gives the share and the total area is one. With unequal widths, compare areas rather than treating heights as probabilities. A smoothed density uses the same area interpretation. For example, 30 of 150 stores in a two-point interval give a share of 0.20 and a density of 0.10 per percentage point.

Mode, percentile range, and relative spread answer additional questions

Three complementary summaries
SummaryDefinitionUse
ModeMost frequent value or categoryIdentify the most common outcome
P90 − P1090th minus 10th percentileSpread of the central 80%
Coefficient of variationSD / meanSpread relative to a positive ratio-scale mean

A dataset can have several equally frequent modes. For near-continuous measurements, an exact-value mode is sensitive to rounding; a modal histogram interval also depends on the bins. P90 minus P10 omits both outer tails. The coefficient of variation is dimensionless, but its interpretation needs a meaningful zero and a positive mean away from zero. It suits relative variation in quantities such as demand; it is not meaningful for arbitrary temperature origins.

Choose displays and comparisons deliberately

General theory

Histograms, densities, and boxplots expose different distribution features

  • Histogram: counts or shares within intervals
  • Density: a smoothed shape with total area one
  • Boxplot: median, quartiles, and a stated whisker rule
  • Skewness and tail weight describe different aspects of shape

A histogram depends on bin boundaries and widths; a density depends on smoothing. A conventional boxplot marks the median and quartiles, with whiskers extending to observations within 1.5 IQR of the box. Values beyond these fences are flagged for inspection. A violin adds a density shape to the same distributional view.

Comparable group displays use consistent scales and denominators

  • Keep measurement definitions and periods aligned
  • Use common bins and axis ranges
  • Use shares or density when group sizes differ
  • Show the number of observations in each group

Raw counts and within-group shares answer different questions. A group can contain more events simply because it has more observations. State the group denominator, preserve category order, and show sample sizes. The aim is to distinguish composition, prevalence, and severity using a comparison that readers can reconstruct.

A conditional mean summarizes the observations sharing a characteristic

E[Y∣X=x]=expected outcome at the specified x

Conditioning narrows the population being summarized. For a categorical X, estimate the conditional mean within each category. For a continuous X, bins or a fitted curve can summarize the relationship. A scatterplot preserves individual variation that group averages can hide.

Correlation standardizes the linear co-movement of two variables

Corr(X,Y)=Cov(X,Y)SD(X)SD(Y)

Covariance is positive when above-average values of one variable tend to coincide with above-average values of the other. Correlation divides by their standard deviations, removing the measurement units and producing a value from −1 to 1. Inspect the scatterplot as well: a nonlinear relationship can have little linear correlation.

Description, prediction, and causal explanation answer different questions

  • Description: what patterns appear in the observed population?
  • Prediction: what outcome should we expect for another observation?
  • Causation: what would change under an intervention?

The same association may be useful for describing groups or anticipating outcomes. To interpret it as the consequence of changing a variable, we also need an account of how that variable is assigned and what else changes with it. The course develops those comparison designs after introducing prediction.

Build association from paired deviations

General theory

Covariance averages products of deviations from the two means

sxy=∑i(xi−x¯)(yi−y¯)n−1;r=sxysxsy

A pair above both means or below both means has a positive product. A pair on opposite sides has a negative product. Adding those signed contributions describes whether the variables move together. Covariance uses the product of the original units; dividing by both standard deviations yields a unit-free correlation.

Here the sample covariance and both sample variances use n−1. A descriptive population convention uses n in all three quantities. Either consistent convention gives the same correlation because the factors cancel. Correlation requires nonzero variation in both variables.

Linear association can be strong, weak, or absent in a curved pattern

Read the direction and dispersion together. All points on an increasing straight line give r = 1; a decreasing straight line gives r = −1. Dispersed points can retain positive co-movement. In the final illustrative panel, Y equals X squared at symmetric X values, so the signed products cancel even though knowing X determines Y. Inspect the scatterplot before interpreting a small correlation.

A pooled correlation and a within-group correlation describe different comparisons

  • Pooled: compare every observation with the overall means
  • Within-group: recalculate means and spread inside each group
  • Report the group definition and observation count
  • Interpret differences through group mix and operating conditions

The pooled coefficient includes both between-group and within-group co-movement. A subgroup coefficient centers and scales using that subgroup. It can therefore differ in sign or magnitude from the pooled value, and is not obtained by simply averaging subgroup correlations. Restricted ranges and small groups also change the comparison. Use the observed pattern to choose the next descriptive question; a causal explanation requires a separate design.

Move from repeated weeks to store profiles

Worked application

Worked application: Baseline · weeks 1–8 · one average per store. Apply the general method to the shared retail records below.

Start with the same repaired weeks 1–8. Average the eight weekly rates within each store. This produces 150 store profiles, each based on the same monitoring basket and number of weeks. The store table adds usual delivery time and urban location without creating extra observations.

The mean store rate is 12.74%; the median is 12.63%. The median puts half the stores on either side. The middle half of stores lies between 11.07% and 14.55%. These summaries answer complementary planning questions: total service burden, a typical store, and how widely the workload varies.

An average can conceal the stores that most often need help. A review queue should therefore retain the store-level rates and their operating context, rather than replacing every row with the chain-wide figure.

Compare two views of the same stores

Worked application

Changing bin width changes detail while preserving the broad concentration

Both panels contain all 150 store averages for weeks 1–8. The horizontal range and vertical percentage scale are identical. Two-point bins show finer local detail; four-point bins merge adjacent intervals and therefore have larger shares. The broad concentration persists. A local bump that appears under one width is a reason to inspect the rows, rather than an established new segment.

A histogram counts stores inside intervals

The horizontal axis is the stockout rate and the vertical axis is a count of stores. Bin boundaries determine which values are combined. Narrow bins show more local detail; wide bins produce a smoother summary. Compare the width-2 and width-4 versions in the lab before deciding that a small bump is an important business segment.

Location and spread answer different questions

Keep centre and variation together
StatisticBaseline valueInterpretation
Mean12.74Arithmetic average
Median12.63Middle store
Sample standard deviation2.39Spread in percentage points
Interquartile range3.48Width of the middle half
Minimum to maximum6.70 to 18.30Full observed range

The mean uses every value and moves with extremes. The median depends on order. Variance averages squared deviations using n−1 in the sample formula; its square root is the standard deviation. The interquartile range uses the 25th and 75th percentiles. These summaries complement one another rather than competing to be the single correct statistic.

Follow the arithmetic behind the spread

Mean=∑ixinSample variance=∑i(xi−mean)2n−1

Standard deviation=variance;IQR=Q3−Q1

For the 150 store averages, sample variance is 5.74 squared percentage points and standard deviation is 2.39 points. Squaring gives large deviations more influence. State the original units when interpreting the square root.

Read a boxplot from the centre outward

  • The line marks the median.
  • The box runs from Q₁ to Q₃.
  • A common rule extends whiskers to observations within 1.5 × IQR.
  • Values beyond those fences are shown individually.

The corresponding fences are 5.85% and 19.78%; 0 store averages fall beyond them. A flagged point deserves investigation, not automatic deletion. A violin adds an estimated density shape; it depends on smoothing, so retain the sample size and observed range.

Compare the quartiles with the smoothed shape

The upper shape is a Gaussian kernel density estimate using the default Scott bandwidth rule. The lower display marks the quartiles, median, and observed range. Its range line is a deliberately labelled alternative to the 1.5-IQR whisker convention. Both displays summarize the same store averages; the density shows estimated shape while the box emphasizes location and spread.

Distinguish skewness from tail weight

Two aspects of distribution shape
Shape measureCalculated valueWhat it describes
Sample skewness0.02Asymmetry around the centre
Excess kurtosis-0.57Tail weight relative to the normal benchmark

A long right tail can make the mean exceed the median. Kurtosis does not simply measure how tall the centre looks. Use the graph, the summary table, and the underlying rows together, especially when there are few extreme stores.

Compare full distributions before prioritizing groups

Worked application

Long-lead stores have a higher centre with overlapping store outcomes

The boxes share a single stockout-rate axis and use one store as the observation. Compare the median lines first, then the quartiles, whiskers, and individual outliers. The long-lead group is shifted upward, but the overlap means delivery group does not determine an individual store’s performance. This supports prioritizing review while still inspecting each store.

Group spread shows how representative each group average is

Store-level baseline rates; all summaries in percentage points except n

Calculate every summary separately within the named group, using the same eight-week baseline and measurement rule. The mean locates the average; SD and IQR report variation around and within the distribution. Read these values with the boxes rather than ranking groups solely by their means. The counts show how much of the chain each comparison represents.

Worked application

Baseline service burden by usual delivery time

For each group, count stores whose baseline rate exceeds the 10% service target. Divide by the number of stores in that group. This denominator answers the manager’s question: how common is the problem among the stores that share this delivery pattern?

Long lead (4–5 days):7879×100=98.73% above target

The mean rate measures severity; the share above target measures how broadly the target is missed. A group could have a few severe outliers or a widespread moderate problem. Showing both gives operations a better basis for allocating review time.

Both views use the same underlying observations. A store can have a high average in a generally difficult week, or a persistent problem across several weeks.

Use the delivery comparison to choose where to investigate the operating process. Ask store teams about replenishment schedules, promotions, and the products most often unavailable. The comparison describes where the burden sits; the alert pilot later measures what a particular action changes.

Inspect individual stores before averaging

Worked application

Individual stores vary substantially around the demand relationship

Each dot joins a store’s average demand to its average stockout rate over weeks 1–8. The upward tendency coexists with substantial variation at similar demand. Follow this with the five-bin display: sorting by demand, forming equal-count groups, and averaging produces a clearer broad pattern while hiding the within-bin spread. Both plots use the same stores; the five averages are not five new observations.

Connect composition and association to the review decision

Worked application

Compare composition within each group

Within-group stockout bands
Delivery groupStoresAt/below 10%10–15%Above 15%
Long lead (4–5 days)791.27%63.29%35.44%
Short lead (2–3 days)7126.76%71.83%1.41%

The percentages in each row sum to 100. A 100% stacked bar would show the same composition, using a consistent order from lower to higher stockout burden. Ordered categories preserve that meaning when tables are reshaped or plotted.

A stacked bar makes the within-group composition visible

The table first counts stores in each ordered stockout band, divides each count by its own delivery-group total, and multiplies by 100. The chart displays those percentages as adjacent segments. Keep the category order and colours consistent across groups. Equal bar lengths compare composition; group counts remain visible beside the bars.

Five quantile bins of baseline demand

Sort stores by baseline demand, divide them into five groups with similar counts, and plot each group’s mean demand against its mean rate. Quantile bins need not have equal widths. The binned points summarize the relationship, while an individual-store scatterplot shows the variation hidden by averaging.

Covariance and correlation quantify co-movement

Correlation=Cov(X,Y)SD(X)SD(Y)

  • Demand–stockout covariance: 9.66
  • Correlation: 0.35

Covariance retains the units of both variables. Correlation standardizes them and lies between −1 and 1. It measures linear association; a value near zero can coexist with a nonlinear relationship. Compare subgroup correlations with their sample sizes, and use the operating process to decide what the relationship might mean.

Reconstruct the association from the shared rows

Worked application

Each store contributes a signed product to the covariance

First four stores; products use unrounded deviations
StoreDemand − meanRate − meanProduct
S001-15.575-3.54655.225
S002-15.361-3.72457.211
S003-1.1681.454-1.699
S004-8.7841.901-16.695

The full-store means are demand 106.152 and rate 12.742%. Subtract those means for every store. Multiply the two deviations in each row. Positive contributions place a store on the same side of both means; negative contributions place it on opposite sides. These four rows illustrate the calculation; the total on the next slide includes all 150 stores.

The full-store product sum yields a positive but dispersed association

Covariance=1439.952149=9.664r=9.66411.414×2.395=0.354

Use all 150 centered products, divide by 149 for sample covariance, and divide again by both sample standard deviations for correlation. Calculations use unrounded values. Covariance is in demand-index units times percentage points; correlation is unit-free. The resulting moderate positive association matches the upward but dispersed individual-store scatter.

Within-group correlations retain their own counts and comparison scope

Pearson correlations recalculated within each delivery group
ComparisonStoresDemand–rate correlation
All stores1500.354

For each row, recalculate the mean demand, mean rate, covariance, and standard deviations using only that row’s stores. Compare these coefficients with the all-store value. They describe association within the delivery categories rather than the full mixture. Use both perspectives when identifying operating questions for regression in later lessons; the coefficients do not measure the effect of changing demand.

The next lesson asks how much confidence to put in a new shelf audit based on a sample of stores. That will let the director weigh the cost of checking every location against the precision of a smaller audit.

Explain, reconstruct, diagnose and transfer

Decision and synthesis

Joint and conditional probabilities answer different denominator questions

  • Use the 2×2 table to calculate the stockout probability, both conditional probabilities, and their weighted average.
  • Someone divides 12 by 100 and calls it P(stockout | long delivery). Explain the denominator mistake and what 12/100 actually measures.

Work independently or explain your reasoning to a partner. State the target, units and assumptions before calculating. The student notebook provides runnable setup and separate task cells; the companion solution checks the calculation. The lesson’s completed lab remains available as a reference, with its steps separated into smaller cells.

Changing the group mix changes the overall mean without changing group risks

  • Keep conditional risks 10% and 30%, but change the long-delivery share to 75%. Calculate the new mean; explain whether this proves delivery causes stockouts.
  • Submit a calculation, an assumption and a justified next action

An acceptable answer can recommend more information, a narrower claim or no action. It must connect the method to the target and explain the consequence of a failed assumption. Use the assessment criteria after attempting the task; matching a supplied recommendation is not the grading objective.

After your attempt: check the reasoning

Open the assessment criteria

Show 18%, 10%, 30%, and .6×.1+.4×.3=.18. Transfer mean is 25%. State the population mix and avoid a causal claim.

Update the decision memo

The mean baseline rate is 12.74%, with the middle half of stores spanning 11.07%–14.55%. Retain group coverage and store IDs in the review list so the alert proposal responds to the actual distribution of service problems.

Make the call

To report the share of long-lead stores above target, which denominator belongs in the calculation?

Compare your reasoning

Use all long-lead stores. Dividing by all 150 stores answers how much of the whole chain belongs to that category, which is a different question.

The bigger picture

The same descriptive tools apply to costs, processing times, customer demand, and service quality. A single average does not show where variation or extreme outcomes occur. Choose a distributional summary and a conditional comparison that answer the question, then use their definitions consistently when allocating attention.

After your decision: open the known answer

All 150 store profiles are calculated from the same eight repaired weekly records per store. The group comparison introduces no new dataset and changes no stockout definition.
